In Los Angeles, the man accused of starting the deadly Palisades fire last year has been
found guilty by a federal jury, Steve Futterman reports.
The jury reached its verdict on the third day of deliberations, finding Jonathan Rinderknecht
guilty on both counts.
He was accused of setting the Lachman fire on January 1st last year, just past midnight.

fire.

For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman at the Federal Courthouse in Los Angeles.
This week, the Senate passed a bipartisan bill meant to overhaul the permitting process
to build new energy projects.
NPR's Matthew Brown reports it could shorten or remove the environmental review processes
now used by federal regulators.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act could bring major changes to American
infrastructure.
It could also narrow the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered
Species Act.
The bill received strong bipartisan support and backing from industry groups representing
renewable energy companies as well as oil and gas suppliers.
But environmental groups are pushing back.
They're concerned that the bill will mostly benefit fossil fuel projects.
And tribal organizations warned that some provisions may restrict their ability to review
projects at culturally significant indigenous sites.
The bill still must pass the House before President Trump signs it.
That may not happen in the crowded final months for this Republican-led Congress.
Matthew Brown, NPR News, Washington.

New York's Mayor Zoran Mondani announced plans Friday to close the city's troubled Rikers
Island jail complex by 2032.
The mayor's plan calls for lowering the jail inmate population from 6,700 currently at
Rikers to about 4,000 and taking those people and moving them to new smaller jails in the
Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn, and Manhattan, as well as some secure medical facilities for
people with health care needs.
Montana's overwhelmingly supported a ballot measure to make political spending more transparent.
Montana Public Radio's Aaron Bolton reports the effort is already facing a legal challenge.
The ballot initiative only allows people to spend on Montana elections.
Corporations and political groups with anonymous donors cannot donate.
The Institute for Free Speech, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit, filed a legal challenge.
The institute argues it violates Citizens United, a controversial U.S. Supreme Court
decision.
That protected businesses and other groups' right to spend on elections.
The nonprofit also filed a legal challenge against a similar law in Hawaii.
Montana's Attorney General Austin Knudsen says he won't defend the proposition in court.
Supporters say they will.
For NPR News, I'm Aaron Bolton in Columbia Falls, Montana.
